question: What is the main purpose of a screen at a raw water intake?
correctAnswer: To keep large debris from entering the intake and damaging downstream equipment
explanation: Intake screens stop logs, branches and other large debris at the entry point, protecting pumps and downstream processes. They do not disinfect, soften or meter the water.
options: To disinfect the raw water before pumping
To remove dissolved minerals from the source water
To measure the raw water flow entering the plant
To keep large debris from entering the intake and damaging downstream equipment

correctAnswer: The coarse bar screen at the intake structure
explanation: Coarse bar screens at the intake structure intercept the largest material first. Finer screening and straining happen later, once the bulky debris has been removed.
options: The fine travelling screen inside the plant
The cartridge filter on the raw water line
The coarse bar screen at the intake structure
The strainer on the treated water discharge

question: How should an intake be positioned in a lake or river source to draw the best available water?
correctAnswer: At a depth and location that avoid surface scum and bottom sediment
explanation: A well placed intake draws from a zone away from floating scum at the surface and settled sediment at the bottom, where raw water quality is usually most consistent.
options: As close to the surface as possible to catch floating algae
Resting on the bottom so sediment seals the opening
At a depth and location that avoid surface scum and bottom sediment
Immediately downstream of a storm sewer outfall

explanation: A growing level difference across a screen signals added head loss, most often from debris or ice blocking part of the screen area and restricting flow.

The raw water has become warmer overnight
The treated water storage tank is full
The screen openings have enlarged with age

question: Why is the velocity of water passing through an intake screen normally kept low?
correctAnswer: To reduce debris being pinned against the screen and harm to aquatic life
explanation: Low approach velocity keeps debris from being pressed firmly onto the screen, makes cleaning easier and reduces the impingement of fish and other aquatic life.

To reduce debris being pinned against the screen and harm to aquatic life
To warm the water before it reaches the plant
To allow dissolved gases to escape at the intake

correctAnswer: To simulate plant coagulation, flocculation and settling on a bench scale so a chemical dose can be selected
explanation: A jar test reproduces the plant mixing and settling sequence in small beakers, letting the operator compare doses and pick the one that forms good floc and clears the water.

To calibrate the plant flow meter
To check the accuracy of the laboratory turbidimeter

correctAnswer: Rapid mix, then slow mix, then settling
explanation: The jar test mirrors the plant: a short rapid mix disperses the chemical, a longer slow mix grows floc, and a quiet settling period shows how well the floc separates.
options: Rapid mix, then slow mix, then settling
Slow mix, then rapid mix, then settling
Settling, then rapid mix, then slow mix
Rapid mix only, with no settling period

question: What is the main goal of the sedimentation step in a conventional treatment plant?
correctAnswer: To remove most of the floc and suspended solids so the filters receive a lighter load
explanation: Sedimentation lets gravity remove the bulk of the floc formed upstream. Filters then polish a much lighter solids load and can run longer between backwashes.
options: To disinfect the water before filtration
To add alkalinity to the water
To remove most of the floc and suspended solids so the filters receive a lighter load
To raise the water temperature before filtration

question: What effect does short-circuiting inside a clarifier have on settled water quality?
correctAnswer: Part of the flow reaches the outlet sooner than the design detention time, so it carries more solids out
explanation: Short-circuiting means some water takes a direct path to the outlet and leaves before its floc can settle, raising settled water turbidity even at normal average flow.
options: It improves settling because the water moves faster
It lowers the sludge blanket uniformly across the basin
It has no effect as long as the average flow is unchanged
Part of the flow reaches the outlet sooner than the design detention time, so it carries more solids out

explanation: Carryover solids load the filter surface and pores faster than design, so head loss climbs quickly and runs end sooner in a backwash.
options: Filter runs become longer and head loss grows more slowly
The filters need no backwashing at all
Filter runs shorten as head loss builds faster from the extra solids
The filter media dissolves more slowly

question: In a dual media filter, why is anthracite placed above the sand layer?
correctAnswer: Anthracite grains are larger and less dense, so the coarser layer stays on top and traps solids through a greater depth
explanation: Anthracite is coarser and lighter than sand, so after backwashing it resettles on top. Water meets large pores first and finer pores later, spreading solids capture through the bed depth.
options: Anthracite is heavier, so it sinks and holds the sand down
Anthracite grains are larger and less dense, so the coarser layer stays on top and traps solids through a greater depth
Anthracite dissolves slowly and releases alkalinity
Anthracite must be shielded from sunlight by the sand

question: What two jobs does a filter underdrain system perform?
correctAnswer: It collects filtered water evenly during filtration and distributes backwash water evenly during washing
explanation: The underdrain works in both directions: it gathers filtrate uniformly so no area of the bed is overloaded, and it spreads backwash flow evenly so the whole bed is cleaned.
options: It heats the backwash water and chlorinates the filtrate
It stores the filter media and meters the coagulant
It supports the raw water pumps and drains the clear well
It collects filtered water evenly during filtration and distributes backwash water evenly during washing

question: Mudballs are found in a filter bed during inspection. What is their most common cause?
correctAnswer: Inadequate backwashing that leaves floc and solids to cement media grains together
explanation: When backwash energy or duration is insufficient, sticky floc is not scoured from the grains and gradually binds them into mudballs that grow and sink into the bed.
options: Backwashing that is too vigorous and too long
Inadequate backwashing that leaves floc and solids to cement media grains together
Using anthracite instead of sand in the bed
Filtering water that is too cold
sourceTitle: US EPA - Surface Water Treatment Rule Turbidity Guidance Manual

The filter run times are too long
The underdrain laterals are too large
The raw water turbidity is too low

question: How is the CT value for disinfection calculated?
correctAnswer: Disinfectant residual in mg/L multiplied by contact time in minutes
explanation: CT is the product of the disinfectant residual concentration and the time the water is exposed to it, expressed as mg/L multiplied by minutes.
options: Disinfectant residual in mg/L multiplied by contact time in minutes
Contact time in minutes divided by the plant flow in L/s
Disinfectant dose in mg/L multiplied by the tank volume in m3
Residual in mg/L divided by the water temperature

question: Winter source water is much colder than summer water. What does this mean for achieving the same disinfection result with chlorine?
correctAnswer: Disinfection reactions slow down, so more CT, through higher residual or longer contact time, is needed
explanation: Cold water slows the chemical reactions that inactivate organisms, so the same level of disinfection requires a greater CT in winter than in warm water.
options: Cold water disinfects faster, so less CT is needed
Temperature has no effect on disinfection
Disinfection reactions slow down, so more CT, through higher residual or longer contact time, is needed
The chlorine residual can be allowed to fall to zero

Because poor baffling lets some water pass through faster, so the effective contact time is shorter than the theoretical value
Because chlorine does not react during the first hour
Because flow meters always over-read at low flow

question: A centrifugal pump is running but delivering no water, and its casing is warm. What is the most likely explanation?
correctAnswer: The pump has lost its prime and is full of air instead of water
explanation: A centrifugal pump cannot move air effectively. If the casing and suction line fill with air, the pump loses prime, delivers nothing and heats up as it churns.
options: The pump has lost its prime and is full of air instead of water
The discharge valve is fully open
The suction water level is at its highest
The motor is rotating too slowly to matter

explanation: When suction pressure falls too low, vapour bubbles form in the liquid and collapse violently on the impeller, producing the gravel noise, vibration and pressure swings of cavitation.

Cavitation, where vapour bubbles form and collapse inside the pump
A fully primed suction line

question: What is the purpose of a check valve on a pump discharge line?
correctAnswer: To prevent flow from running backward through the pump when it stops

To filter solids out of the pumped water

correctAnswer: Priming fills the casing and suction line with water so the impeller can create the low pressure needed to lift more water

question: An operator is collecting a bacteriological sample from a plant sample tap. Which practice is correct?

Grab samples use less water than composite samples
Regulations forbid the use of automatic samplers anywhere in a plant

question: What does a turbidity measurement actually describe?

question: Immediately after a filter is returned to service following a backwash, its effluent turbidity is briefly elevated before improving. What is this period called, and how is it commonly managed?
correctAnswer: Filter ripening, often managed by sending the initial filtrate to waste until quality recovers
explanation: A freshly washed bed needs a short ripening period while its pores begin capturing particles again. Filtering to waste during that window keeps the poorer quality water out of the clear well.
options: Filter ripening, often managed by sending the initial filtrate to waste until quality recovers
Filter starvation, managed by raising the coagulant dose sharply
Media cementing, managed by replacing the top layer of sand
Air binding, managed by venting the clear well
sourceTitle: US EPA - Surface Water Treatment Rule Turbidity Guidance Manual
